We pay our respects to their elders past and present and extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples today. Hey Coaches, our next presenter is Martin Rocker. Martin is a world leader and innovator in the space of blue to green stage development within our sport, presenting at a multitude of conferences in Europe and Asia. Today Martin joins us to share some of his insights into the orange ball stage of development within our sport. Martin, welcome. Martin Rocker here saying hi to all of you from Girona, Spain. I'm happy to be here presenting my work with Nirokes especially in development ages, which is the work that I enjoy the most. We're going to talk about orange ball stage today, very important phase of the development for the kids. If we talk about what they do in foam ball stages or red ball, sometimes I consider that they are too technical for the kids and then coaches are focused on teaching the technique which is a noble idea, I understand, but according to my views, that makes the sessions too slow, too boring sometimes because if you focus on technique with little kids, they're not able to manage their body correctly and they need to learn a lot about motor skills using implements in our case and our sport, we use tennis racket and tennis ball.

If they don't know how to handle that, trying to be too technical, it makes the sessions a little bit boring and too slow. I want sessions more dynamic. So in my opinion, in those two phases, our focus should be on working on the motor skills, letting the kids be able to express themselves using an implement like a tennis racket and then the main goal should be having the kids be able to rally by themselves. Start with floor tennis, start rallying with no net, eventually moving on to having the net in between and being able to rally. That's when they should be considered themselves as meaning players because they're starting to start to play tennis correctly. So moving on to the orange ball stage, the focus should be on, okay, we have the kids rally but we have to add some stuff now. We're going to work on footwork, we're going to let them move around the mini tennis court and then we have to teach them how to do that correctly. In my, according to my views, we have to focus on balance. We have to teach them how to move around for hands or back hands by always keeping the balance, always trying to control the body and control the movement. So once you get in a good position, you are able to get a good shot, recover and then be able to keep on, to be able to continue the rally. The other key part of this space is the introduction to proper technique in different shots. For example, I do a lot of work, especially in the warm-ups, with continental grip.

The continental grip progressions allow me to have my kids using this grip. Sometimes if they are new in the group, they hold the racket from the top of the grip and then they hit the ball with no net in between. They're rallying like that and that allows them to get to know how to use their wrist, how to use the racket with that grip, and eventually it's easy for me to teach them how to do ballies, how to do overheads, the progressions on serves, and slice. I have a lot of videos that I'm going to show you now and I'm going to let the video do the talking and you'll see the way we do these progressions, the way we work on footwork and the progressions to introduce new techniques and you see the kids having fun, dynamic sessions, and learning a lot of technique progressively, not rushing the process because this is the most important thing for me, going slow, but making sure that every step we take is based on solid ground. As you can see in the videos, all the warm-ups are set up to build team spirit, teamwork, not rewarding only the more skillful kids and trying to have a dynamic session from the beginning. This is a fun game, but it leads to what I do most with the kids is working on balance, working stability when they move and get ready for the next shot in a good position. Allow yourself to be creative and also enjoy the process. This has to be fun not only for the kids, but for the coaches too.
